entry: Greek island in the southern [[Aegean Sea]], the southernmost of the Cyclades (pop., 2021: 15,480). It is the largest island of a small, circular archipelago formed by a [[Caldera|caldera]], with an area of about 73 sq km (28 sq mi). About 3,600 years ago, one of the largest eruptions in recorded history struck the island during the height of the [[Minoan civilization]], leaving a large water-filled caldera surrounded by deep ash deposits. Excavations at Akrotiri have made it the best-known Minoan site outside [[Crete]]. It has been suggested that the eruption inspired the legend of [[Atlantis]].

Public research university in [[Rome]], Italy, one of the world's oldest universities and the largest in Europe, with over 110,000 students. It was founded on April 20, 1303, by decree of [[Pope Boniface VIII]] as a studium for ecclesiastical studies. In 1431 Pope Eugene IV reorganized it to include the schools of Law, Medicine and Philosophy alongside Theology. The name Sapienza, meaning "wisdom" or "knowledge," was used from the 1650s. After the [[Kingdom of Italy]] captured Rome in 1870, the university expanded as the main university of the capital. It teaches all pure and applied sciences and [[Humanities|humanities]]. The university houses 50 libraries, 19 museums and three university hospitals. Its alumni include 10 Nobel laureates and several Italian prime ministers. Since June 2026 it has had an international campus in [[Wuhan]], China, focused on law and economics.

Gem variety of the mineral [[Corundum|corundum]], consisting of aluminum oxide with trace amounts of iron, titanium, cobalt, chromium and other elements. Blue is the best-known color, but sapphires also occur in yellow, purple, orange, and green, and red corundum is called [[Ruby|ruby]]. The name derives from Latin sapphirus, from Greek sappheiros, which referred to [[Lapis lazuli]]. It scores 9 on the [[Mohs scale]], the third-hardest mineral after diamond and moissanite. Natural sapphires are cut into gemstones for jewelry, and synthetic stones are grown in laboratories. Non-ornamental uses include infrared optical components, high-durability windows, wristwatch crystals and the insulating substrates of [[Integrated circuit|integrated circuits]] and blue LEDs.

[[Ancient Greek]] lyric poet from Eresos or Mytilene on the island of [[Lesbos]]. She was widely regarded in antiquity as one of the greatest lyric poets and was given names such as the "Tenth Muse." Most of her poetry has been lost, and only "Ode to Aphrodite" is certainly complete. Her poems were written to be sung to music and were best known in antiquity for their love poetry; other themes include family and religion. Her works are noted for clarity of language and vivid images. Sappho was among the canon of Nine Lyric Poets esteemed by scholars of Hellenistic Alexandria. Beyond her poetry, she is a symbol of love and desire between women: the English words sapphic and lesbian derive from her name and that of her home island.

City, capital of [[Hokkaido]] Prefecture in northern [[Japan]] (pop., 2026: 1,962,596). It lies on an [[Alluvial fan|alluvial fan]] of the Toyohira River and is the largest city in Hokkaido. The area was once a sparsely inhabited plain of the indigenous [[Ainu people|Ainu]]. The city began as an administrative center in 1869 with the establishment of the Hokkaido Development Commission headquarters, and it adopted a grid plan inspired by [[Kyoto]] and Heijō-kyō. After [[World War II]] it replaced Otaru as Hokkaido's commercial hub. The city hosted the 1972 Winter Olympics, the first Winter Olympics held in Asia. Its annual Sapporo Snow Festival draws more than 2 million tourists. Hokkaido University lies just north of Sapporo Station.

Khoekhoe woman exhibited as a freak show attraction in 19th-century Europe as the "Hottentot Venus," a term now regarded as offensive. Born near the Gamtoos River in what is now the Eastern Cape of [[South Africa]], she worked on Dutch farms and as a washerwoman in [[Cape Town]]. In 1810 she was taken to London for exhibition, and later to [[Paris]]. After her death, the naturalist [[Georges Cuvier|Cuvier]] dissected her body, and her remains were displayed at the Musée de l'Homme until repatriation and reburial in Hankey in 2002. Her story has been called the epitome of racist colonial exploitation.

French stage actress who starred in some of the most popular French plays of the late 19th and early 20th centuries. Her roles included *Ruy Blas* by [[Victor Hugo]], *La Dame aux Camélias* by [[Alexandre Dumas|Alexandre Dumas fils]] and *L'Aiglon* by Edmond Rostand. She played female and male roles, including Shakespeare's Hamlet. She made several theatrical tours worldwide and was one of the first prominent actresses to make sound recordings and appear in motion pictures. She was also an accomplished painter and sculptor. At the height of her fame she commissioned the first lithographic theater poster from the then-unknown Alphonse Mucha, who became a sought-after artist of the [[Art Nouveau]] style.

American actress and television producer. She made her Broadway debut at age 11 in the 1976 revival of *The Innocents* and starred in the title role of the musical *Annie* in 1979. Her portrayal of Carrie Bradshaw in the [[HBO]] series *Sex and the City* (1998–2004) won her two Primetime Emmy Awards and four Golden Globe Awards. Her films include *Hocus Pocus* (1993), *Ed Wood* (1994) and *Mars Attacks!* (1996). Since 2005 she has run her own production company, Pretty Matches. [[Time (magazine)|Time magazine]] named her one of the 100 most influential people in the world in 2022.

American actress known for strong female characters in film and television and regarded as a scream queen. She won a Daytime Emmy Award for her role as Kendall Hart on the soap opera *All My Children*. She is best known for playing Buffy Summers in [[Buffy the Vampire Slayer]]. Her film credits include *I Know What You Did Last Summer* (1997), *Scream 2* (1997), *Cruel Intentions* (1999) and *Scooby-Doo* (2002). She co-founded Foodstirs, an [[E-commerce|e-commerce]] baking company that operated from 2015 to 2022.

American [[Stand-up comedy|stand-up comedian]], actress and writer whose satirical work addresses social taboos, including racism, sexism, homophobia, politics and religion. She was a writer and cast member on the [[NBC]] sketch comedy series [[Saturday Night Live]] in 1993 and 1994. She starred in and produced *The Sarah Silverman Program* on Comedy Central from 2007 to 2010, and was nominated for a Primetime Emmy Award. She voiced Vanellope von Schweetz in *Wreck-It Ralph* (2012). During the 2016 United States presidential election she campaigned for [[Bernie Sanders]] before speaking in support of [[Hillary Clinton]] at the Democratic National Convention.

Capital and largest city of [[Bosnia and Herzegovina]], in a valley surrounded by the Dinaric Alps along the Miljacka River in the [[Balkans]]. The modern city arose in the 15th century as an [[Ottoman Empire|Ottoman]] stronghold. In 1914 the assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand by [[Gavrilo Princip]] sparked [[World War I]]. Sarajevo hosted the 1984 Winter Olympics. From April 1992 to February 1996 it endured a siege of 1,425 days during the [[Bosnian War]], the longest siege of a capital city in modern history. The city is sometimes called the "Jerusalem of Europe" and is one of few major European cities with a mosque, a Catholic church, an Eastern Orthodox church and a synagogue in the same neighborhood. In October 2019 [[UNESCO]] designated it a Creative City, and in October 2024 [[National Geographic]] named it the best world destination for 2025 according to its readers.

Principal [[Hinduism|Hindu]] goddess of knowledge, education, learning, speech, arts, music and creativity. She forms the trinity of chief goddesses known as the Tridevi, with [[Lakshmi]] and [[Parvati]]. Saraswati is also venerated in [[Jainism]] and [[Buddhism]]. In the [[Vedas|Vedic]] tradition she is closely connected with the Saraswati River, and later she is identified with the goddess of speech, Vac. She is linked to [[Brahma]] as his creation or consort, and within [[Shaktism]] she is venerated as the creative aspect of the Supreme Goddess. She is portrayed in white with four arms, holding a book, a rosary, a water pot and a veena. Students honor her on Vasant Panchami, when young children traditionally learn to write the letters of the alphabet.

Rare [[Cancer|cancer]] that arises from cells of mesenchymal origin in [[Connective tissue|connective tissues]] such as [[Bone|bone]], [[Cartilage|cartilage]], muscle, fat or vascular tissue. Sarcomas make up about 1% of adult cancer diagnoses and 15% of childhood cancer diagnoses. Common subtypes include liposarcoma, leiomyosarcoma and osteosarcoma. The word derives from the Greek *sarkōma*, "fleshy excrescence or substance," from *sarx*, "flesh." Treatment centers on surgical removal, often supplemented by [[Radiation therapy|radiation therapy]] and, for high-grade cases, [[Chemotherapy|chemotherapy]].

Smallest functional unit of striated [[Skeletal muscle|muscle]] tissue, the repeating segment between two Z-lines in a myofibril. Myofibrils appear under the microscope as alternating dark and light bands. Sarcomeres are made of long, fibrous proteins that slide past each other as a [[Muscle contraction|muscle contracts]] or relaxes. Myosin forms the thick filament and actin the thin filament. The myosin head binds to actin and uses ATP as its energy source, but it can bind only when calcium ions expose the binding sites on actin. The giant protein titin, described as the biggest single highly elasticated protein in nature, extends from the Z-line to the M-band and acts as a sarcomeric ruler. Sarcomeres give skeletal and cardiac muscle its striated appearance, but the myofibrils of smooth muscle are not arranged into sarcomeres.

Clade of [[Vertebrate|vertebrate]] animals comprising the lobe-finned fishes and all four-limbed land animals, or [[Tetrapod|tetrapods]]. In contrast to the [[Actinopterygii]], whose fins are supported only by bony spines, lobe-finned fish have fleshy, muscular lobes in their fins supported by internal bones. Sarcopterygii emerged in the Silurian and early Devonian periods as entirely aquatic species. Their lobed fins evolved into limbs, and the foregut evolved into air-breathing lungs, enabling tetrapods to colonize land. Most lobe-finned fish are extinct; during the Carboniferous and [[Permian]] periods they were dominant predators of freshwater ecosystems. The [[Permian–Triassic extinction event]] hit them especially hard. Today the only living non-tetrapod sarcopterygians are two species of [[Coelacanth|coelacanths]] and six species of [[Lungfish|lungfishes]].

Common name for various small, oily forage fish in the [[Herring|herring]] suborder Clupeoidei. The terms are not precise: the United Kingdom's Sea Fish Industry Authority classifies sardines as young pilchards, and fish shorter than 15 cm (6 in) are sardines. The FAO/WHO Codex standard for canned sardines cites 21 species. The word first appeared in English in the 15th century, possibly referring to [[Sardinia]]. Sardines feed almost exclusively on [[Plankton|zooplankton]] and are caught mainly at night with encircling nets. They are eaten fresh, canned or preserved, and are a source of protein and omega-3 fatty acids. Sardine oil is used in [[Paint|paint]], varnish and linoleum.

Island in the [[Mediterranean Sea]] and one of the twenty regions of [[Italy]]. It is the second-largest island in the Mediterranean after [[Sicily]], lying west of the Italian Peninsula, north of [[Tunisia]] and south of [[Corsica]]. Cagliari is the capital and largest city, and Sardinia has over 1.5 million inhabitants as of 2026. The island's most notable historic culture is the Nuragic civilization, which left more than 7,000 megalithic towers known as nuraghes. Parts of the island were conquered by [[Carthage]] in the late 6th century BC and by [[Rome]] in 238 BC. The Iberian Crown of Aragon consolidated it into the Kingdom of Sardinia in 1324. Sardinian and the Algherese dialect of Catalan are two of Italy's twelve officially protected minority languages.

Region of the [[Atlantic Ocean]] bounded by four currents forming an ocean gyre, and the only named sea without land boundaries. It is distinguished by brown *Sargassum* [[Seaweed|seaweed]] and calm blue waters, with underwater visibility of up to 60 m (200 ft). The [[Gulf Stream]] bounds it on the west, the North Atlantic Current on the north, the Canary Current on the east and the North Atlantic Equatorial Current on the south. [[Christopher Columbus]] wrote in 1492 that the seaweed could trap his ship. The 1920–1922 Dana expeditions determined that the breeding sites of the European eel were in the sea, and the larvae of European and American eels hatch there. [[Bermuda]] lies near its western fringes.

Founder of the [[Akkadian Empire]], known for his conquests of the Sumerian city-states around 2300 BC. He was ruler of the small city of Akkad in central [[Mesopotamia]] and overthrew the established order in the north of Lower Mesopotamia. He then defeated the king of [[Uruk]] and brought [[Sumer]] under Akkadian control. He undertook military expeditions toward the Iranian Plateau, into [[Elam]], and toward [[Syria]], though he did not incorporate those territories into his kingdom. He is sometimes identified as the first person in recorded history to rule over an empire. His reign is poorly understood, and later legends about him mix fact with invention.

Large [[Confederation|confederation]] of ancient Iranian equestrian nomadic peoples who dominated the Pontic steppe from around the 5th century BC to the 4th century AD. Originating in the Eurasian Steppe, they formed part of the wider [[Scythians|Scythian]] cultures and came to dominate them by 200 BC. At their greatest reported extent, around 100 BC, they ranged from the [[Danube]] eastward to the [[Volga]], bordering the Black and Caspian seas and the Caucasus. In the 1st century AD they began encroaching on the [[Roman Empire]] in alliance with Germanic tribes. In the 3rd century the [[Goths]] broke their dominance of the Pontic steppe. With the Hunnic invasions of the 4th century, many joined the Goths and [[Vandals]] and settled in the Western Roman Empire. The Alans survived into the Early Middle Ages and gave rise to the modern Ossetic ethnic group.

Last pre-Islamic Iranian empire, ruled by the House of Sasan from 224 to 651 AD. Lasting over four centuries, it was second in length only to the [[Parthian Empire]] that preceded it. Its rulers sought to restore the legacy of the [[Achaemenid Empire]]. At its zenith the empire controlled all of modern [[Iran]], Iraq, parts of the [[Arabian Peninsula]], the [[Caucasus]], the Levant, and parts of Central Asia and the Indian subcontinent. [[Ctesiphon]] was its capital for all but the first two years of its existence. The empire revived [[Zoroastrianism]] as a legitimizing and unifying ideal, and its cultural influence reached Western Europe, East Africa, China and India. It fell to the early Muslim conquests after a devastating war with the [[Byzantine Empire]].

American actress, musician and writer, and former [[Pornographic film|pornographic film]] actress. She won 15 awards for her work in the industry between 2007 and 2010, including the AVN Award for Female Performer of the Year in 2008. She starred in [[Steven Soderbergh]]'s *The Girlfriend Experience* (2009), and later appeared in *Open Windows* and *Would You Rather*. In 2011 she played a fictionalized version of herself in the [[HBO]] series *Entourage*. She co-founded the industrial music band aTelecine and wrote *The Juliette Society* trilogy of novels.

Province of western [[Canada]], landlocked along with [[Alberta]] and bordered by [[Manitoba]] to the east (pop., 2026: 1,278,402). Nearly 10% of its 651,900 sq km (251,700 sq mi) is fresh water. Most people live in the southern [[Prairie|prairie]] half, and roughly half live in [[Saskatoon]] and Regina, the capital. The economy is based on agriculture, mining and energy. Europeans first settled the area in 1774, and it became a province on September 1, 1905. In the early 20th century it became a stronghold of [[Social democracy|social democracy]], and in 1944 it elected North America's first socialist government.

Largest city in the Canadian province of [[Saskatchewan]], straddling a bend in the South Saskatchewan River (pop., 2021: 266,141). Founded in 1882 as a temperance colony by the [[Toronto]]-based Temperance Colonization Society, it is the cultural and economic hub of central Saskatchewan. It is home to the University of Saskatchewan and to Wanuskewin Heritage Park, a National Historic Site representing 6,000 years of First Nations history and a [[UNESCO]] World Heritage applicant. The city is named after the saskatoon berry, native to the region. Its nicknames include "Paris of the Prairies" and "The City of Bridges."

Entity in [[Abrahamic religions]] who entices humans into sin or falsehood, also known as the Devil. In [[Judaism]], Satan is an agent subservient to God, and in the [[Hebrew Bible]] he is a heavenly prosecutor who tests the loyalty of Yahweh's followers. In [[Christianity]] and [[Islam]] he is usually seen as a fallen angel or [[Jinn|jinn]] who rebelled against God. In the [[Book of Revelation]], Satan appears as a Great Red Dragon who is defeated and cast into the Lake of Fire. In the Quran, Iblis refuses to bow before Adam and is cast out of Heaven. During the early modern period Satan's significance grew as beliefs in demonic possession and witchcraft spread, though [[Voltaire]] criticized belief in Satan during the Age of Enlightenment.
